children.value: Transformers come in three families that differ in their attention mask: encoders see the whole input and suit classification and embeddings, decoders see only the past and generate text, and encoder-decoders transform one sequence into another, as in translation and speech recognition.

Encoders are pretrained with masked language modeling, decoders with causal language modeling, encoder-decoders with span corruption or denoising, and embedding models with contrastive objectives. Distillation produces small models from large ones.
Today’s transformers share pre-normalization, rotary position embeddings, gated feed-forward layers, and grouped-query attention, and large models increasingly use mixtures of experts.

Fine-tuning adds a small head, for sequence classification, token classification, or span extraction, and continues training with small learning rates. A frozen encoder is cheap and shareable; full fine-tuning is more accurate; LoRA trains a fraction of a percent of the parameters with similar results.

On the NLTK tweets, Naive Bayes reaches 99.85% because the labels are the emoticons by which the tweets were collected. Without emoticons, Naive Bayes and a frozen encoder reach 79%, a fine-tuned encoder 83%, zero-shot prototypes 68%, and a prompt to Claude Sonnet 79% (Haiku 75%) without any labeled example; on 17% of the tweets, both language models disagree with the label, because the sentiment was in the removed emoticon. The most important check comes before any classifier: how were the labels made?

Among methods of similar accuracy, choose the simplest (Occam’s razor). Naive Bayes trains in milliseconds and classifies a tweet in microseconds, about 300,000 times faster than a prompt to a large model, and the four points of the fine-tuned encoder may not survive other data.

A generative model produces text by repeatedly sampling the next token. Temperature and top-p sampling shape the distribution; greedy decoding is deterministic. Fluent but false continuations, hallucinations, follow from the mechanism.

Instruction tuning and preference alignment turn a language model into an assistant, which expects its input in a chat template. The KV cache stores the keys and values of past tokens and dominates the memory for long contexts.

Prompts classify and extract without training, can follow new instructions immediately, and can be forced into valid JSON by constrained decoding, but they are slow and costly per request, and the confidences they write are not probabilities.
